thread.title: Why Apple's decision feels like a complete rebuke of North Carolina

author: Sougata Mukherjee
title: Why Apple's decision feels like a complete rebuke of North Carolina
text: – Editor, Triangle Business Journal Dec 14, 2018, 8:45am EST In a complete rebuke of North Carolina, Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL) announced Thursday that it will be building a $1 billion campus in Austin, Texas, that one day will house some 15,000 workers. To make all of us wonder what we did wrong in the past few months, the company also announced it plans to add new sites in Seattle, San Diego and Culver City, California. But wait! That's not all — the iPhone maker also announced Pittsburgh, New York and Boulder, Colorado, better be ready for expansion, with new jobs in their cities. Just weeks ago, Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ: AMZN) bypassed the Triangle and chose the Washington, D.C., and New York City metros to split its East Coast headquarters. So we lost both these projects. The Amazon loss was really inconsequential, since nobody in the know really thought we would get it in the first place. But Apple? This was supposed to be a done deal. CEO Tim Cook 's deep ties to Duke University and COO Jeff Williams ' family ties to Raleigh (he went to Sanderson High School and N.C. State University) were game-changers for this project, right? In May, when we first reported that first reported that Apple was looking at the Triangle , noise got so loud that some of our colleagues in the media started saying this is a "done deal" — and many of us started believing. So, what happened in the last six months that changed the course of this project? I can think of a few things. Let's quickly analyze the plausibility of these factors. • Cook and his team could not find a suitable location in the Triangle to build a giant campus . We know the company was looking at land in Research Triangle Park and temporary facilities in Cary and Raleigh. It's hard to believe, given Gov. Roy Cooper's interest in recruiting Apple, that the Research Triangle Foundation could not get its covenants or other restrictions loosened to accommodate the iPhone maker. • Not enough skilled workers. Well, if that is true, then we all have been living a lie. We have been told for years that our area is smart, educated and ripe with skilled labor. The market features three major universities pumping out graduates every year, and numbers from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and recent analysis from Brookings reflect our labor force can compete with the best communities in the world. • Not enough incentives . It is possible the company was looking for big dollars from the state. And details on some major relocation projects show Texas can be creative with its corporate incentives package. Let's not also forget that Texas has no income tax. So, great for employees. But I am not sure that was the driving factor in Apple's decision not to pick North Carolina. Remember, the company did not pick us — for anything. Surely, we could have beaten Pittsburgh, Boulder, San Diego or even New York for a smaller expansion that required smaller incentives that could have passed muster among our lawmakers and economic developers. North Carolina even changed the law earlier this year to make sure Apple was aware of this "transformational projects" clause added to its incentives policy. So why would a company that was serious about North Carolina early on walk away in the end? • North Carolina legislature: Led by Cook and attested by its workforce, Apple has been concerned about several things that have happened with the North Carolina General Assembly in recent years — starting with the infamous bathroom bill, aka House Bill 2. That saga ended in 2017, but publicly released documents from other projects show site-selection people still bring up HB2. And then this year, voters were asked to weigh in on six amendments — from voter ID to hunting access to limiting the power of our governor. Four of the six amendments passed. When North Carolina's pitch and correspondence surrounding this project becomes public, we will know the level of concern from folks in Cupertino, California. But let's just understand that Texas has voter ID laws as well. In fact, they had one of the strictest laws in the nation when it went into effect in 2013. But last year, the legislature passed a softer version of the voter ID law, Senate Bill 5, that held up in courts after groups protested the new law is still not enough to avoid voter suppression. In the past few days, we have had at least one government official reach out to us arguing politics is not playing a role in Apple's decision. In fact, the caller, who did not want to identified but said he was representing one of the Republican leaders, argued that media is making up this narrative about Apple's hesitation in making a decision. He may be right — but we will soon find out when the economic development package is released. And, I hope at some point, Apple tackles this situation head on. It will help all of us moving forward. What gives me pause about this decision from Apple is that it looks like the company went out of its way to make sure North Carolina did not get anything. The news release mentioned seven different localities that will either get new facilities or expansions for existing facilities. How does one fall from being a favorite to being an also-ran with Toledo, Wichita Falls and Beaumont, Texas? (I made up these names for effect. Bless their hearts — Toledo, Wichita Falls and Beaumont are fine towns. So, no emails please.) Seriously, was there a message being sent? It certainly will be interesting to hear the take from some of our local economic developers next week, when they are scheduled to talk about the lessons learned from the Amazon HQ2 process . We are certainly going to add the Apple sidebar to that discussion. Whatever it is, this one hurts — bad. As one of the executives from a tech concern texted me this week: "We are close. But we are not there yet."
